summary.text: For the listed value \(n=67\), the two distinct integers \(147\) and \(2055\) both yield residue sums equal to \(67\): \(1+3+3+3+19+19+19=67\) and \(1+3+9\cdot7=67\), respectively. Thus \(67\) occurs at least twice, contradicting the claimed multiplicity one.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
F(m)=\sum_{k=1}^{\lfloor \log_2 m\rfloor}(m\bmod 2^k).
\]
Thus A049802 is the sequence whose value at the index \(m\) is \(F(m)\), and \(a(n)\) is the number of indices \(m\) for which \(F(m)=n\). In the stated finite formulation, for \(n>0\),
\[
a(n)=\#\bigl\{m:0\le m<2^{n+1}\text{ and }F(m)=n\bigr\};
\]
the bound \(2^{n+1}\) is sufficient for counting all occurrences. For the disproof, it is enough to find two distinct indices inside this range having the same value \(67\).

We use
\[
m_1=147=2^7+19
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
m_2=2055=2^{11}+7.
\]
We compute \(F(m_1)\) first. Since
\[
2^7=128\le 147<256=2^8,
\]
we have \(\lfloor\log_2 147\rfloor=7\), so the defining sum has the seven terms corresponding to \(k=1,\ldots,7\). Their values are
\[
\begin{aligned}
147\bmod 2&=1,\\
147\bmod 4&=3,\\
147\bmod 8&=3,\\
147\bmod 16&=3,\\
147\bmod 32&=19,\\
147\bmod 64&=19,\\
147\bmod 128&=19.
\end{aligned}
\]
Indeed, for the first four moduli these follow respectively from
\(147=73\cdot2+1\), \(147=36\cdot4+3\), \(147=18\cdot8+3\), and \(147=9\cdot16+3\). For the last three, use
\(147=4\cdot32+19=2\cdot64+19=1\cdot128+19\), with \(19\) smaller than each relevant modulus. Consequently,
\[
F(147)=1+3+3+3+19+19+19=67.
\]

Next consider \(m_2=2055\). Since
\[
2^{11}=2048\le2055<4096=2^{12},
\]
we have \(\lfloor\log_2 2055\rfloor=11\). Hence \(F(2055)\) is the sum of the eleven remainders modulo \(2^k\), for \(1\le k\le11\). The first two are
\[
2055\bmod2=1,
\qquad
2055\bmod4=3.
\]
For every \(k\) with \(3\le k\le11\), the number \(2^k\) divides \(2^{11}=2048\). Since \(2055=2048+7\) and \(0\le7<2^k\), it follows that
\[
2055\bmod2^k=7
\qquad(3\le k\le11).
\]
There are \(11-3+1=9\) such values of \(k\). Therefore
\[
F(2055)=1+3+9\cdot7=1+3+63=67.
\]

Both indices are included in the finite set used to define \(a(67)\): indeed,
\[
147<2^{68}
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
2055<2^{68},
\]
for example because both are already less than \(2^{12}\), while \(12<68\). Thus the set
\[
T=\bigl\{m:0\le m<2^{68}\text{ and }F(m)=67\bigr\}
\]
contains both \(147\) and \(2055\). These are distinct, since \(147\ne2055\). Hence \(T\) has at least two elements, and so
\[
a(67)=\#T\ge2.
\]
In particular, \(a(67)\ne1\).

Finally, \(67\) belongs to the set
\[
\{1,3,5,9,15,23,35,63,65,67\}.
\]
Therefore the conjecture that \(a(n)=1\) for every \(n\) in this set would imply \(a(67)=1\), contradicting the two distinct occurrences exhibited above. The conjecture is thus false.
